chunks: "A multiphase buck is several buck power stages, called phases, that all feed the same output capacitor and load but are switched at staggered times.
With N phases the clocks are offset by one N-th of a switching period, so a 4-phase converter turns on a new phase every 90 degrees.
Each phase has its own inductor and its own pair of FETs, and each carries about one N-th of the load current. At the output the inductor currents add up.

Because the triangular ripples are shifted in time, they partly cancel, so the ripple current going into the output capacitor is smaller than one phase's ripple, and it comes at N times the switching frequency.

You get several things out of that one idea: more total current than one inductor and one pair of FETs can handle, much less ripple for a given inductance and capacitance, a faster response to load steps because the effective inductance is L over N, and heat spread over several spots instead of one.
The price is more parts, a controller that has to balance the currents, and a harder layout.
My go-to example is a CPU core supply: 12 volts down to about 1 volts at 60 amps or more, built from four to eight phases."
